corrections: Replaced the approximate heap-height histogram written as an exact finite inequality with the valid sum over floor(n / 2^h) nodes reaching each descent height; applied it to both lesson and question.
Included the initial quicksort stack frame in a safe floor(log2(n)) + 1 bound; preserved the million-element answer of about twenty frames.

Removed the false claim that maximum displacement three means every inversion partner lies within three positions. Bound inversions by total absolute displacement instead; checked every permutation through seven elements.
Separated insertion-sort growth proxies from actual instruction counts. The four-million figure is a bound on n plus inversions, not a literal timing or step count.
Preserved finite rounding allowances in median-of-medians recursion and separated the conservative 294-element exclusion bound from an actual observed count. The 706 answer remains unchanged.
Used ceiling for general radix digit widths; the 32-bit/base-256 and 64-bit/base-256 exact pass examples remain unchanged.
Hedged cache-fit and radix-base speed claims using representation, workload and hardware assumptions. Removed the unsupported universal radix-base sweet spot.
Stated that heap rejection frequency depends on arrival order, and that logarithmic growth proxies compare different operations rather than measured runtime factors.
Clarified compare-by-key labelled records for the insertion-stability question; default Python tuple ordering would also compare the labels.

Added local teaching for Java binarySearch insertion encoding, JavaScript default string ordering, deterministic SQL pagination ties, nearest-bound queries and NumPy partition mutation/order contracts.
Moved the original non-comparison applicability question after bucket-sort teaching. Its former signed/string encoding unit now has a small focused sign-bit question.

Corrected ten old glossary objects: work_mem hash multipliers/multiple budgets, single-partition versus complete Lomuto quicksort cost, Hoare swap-model caveats, versioned minrun, nonunique insertion positions, nonmandated partial_sort implementations, NumPy ties/copy semantics, top-k at one item, adaptive alias coverage, and precise rabbit/turtle aliases.
Added two narrow glossary entries for databases and key comparisons, reused existing two’s-complement/XOR entries elsewhere, and left 182 original glossary objects unchanged.

Converted/reworded inherited inline mathematical derivations and table equations while retaining the worked card mathematics; added explicit grouping and conventional implicit scalar products. corrections: sort-heap-practical-cost: "roughly 45% more comparisons than randomised quicksort" was the leading-term ratio (2 / 1.386 = 1.44) presented as the practical figure → prose now states the simulated count of the lesson heapsort at 10^6 shuffled keys (about 37 million, 1.85n log2 n) against quicksort's 25 million expectation (ratio about 1.5; 1.52 at 65,536) and labels 1.44 as the leading-term ratio; reference card definitions and In words aligned.
sort-merge-theorem-counts: "merge sort needs about 20 million comparisons in the worst case" for 10^6 → about 19 million (exact top-down worst case 18,951,425, as the bound-limits unit says).
sort-heapsort-lower-bound-q8 distractor [3]: "Merge sort needs only about 20 million here" → "at most about 19 million".

sort-timsort-merge-policy: attributed O(n) sorting of two concatenated sorted lists to galloping → run detection finds two runs and one linear merge does it; galloping only cuts that merge's comparisons further.
sort-introsort-fallback: "sub-arrays below a threshold (16 elements in libstdc++)" → "16 elements or fewer" (libstdc++ loops while size > _S_threshold = 16) with one final insertion pass.

sort-timsort-natural-runs: "the sort in Android, V8 ... and Swift" overstated Swift → object sort in Java 7 and Android libcore, V8 since 7.0 (2018), Swift uses a Timsort-style run-merging design (source read).

sort-key-caching: the only statement that a key function costs memory (one stored key per element) was inside the collapsed analogy → added visible prose (CPython keeps the computed keys in a separate array).
editorial: Wrong-sense dictionary links from changed text reworded: "the edges" in sort-selection-q9 (dsa/04 edge-dsa), "successor" in sort-library-hybrids (dsa/02 linked-list successor), "sentinel" in sort-comparator-ordering (dsa/02 sentinel-node), and the analogy's "lower bound/upper bound" in sort-search-insertion-bounds (now "binary-search lower/upper bound", this module's lower_bound entries).

sort-merge-choosing: libstdc++ stable_sort chunk of 7 qualified with "when it can allocate a merge buffer" (without a buffer __inplace_stable_sort insertion-sorts below 15); CPython wording now "extends short runs to a minimum of 32 to 64". sort-pivot-costs prose now gives the 18 million perfect-median comparison next to 25 million. sort-heap-linear-build extraction sentence reworded. sort-heapsort-lower-bound-q7 dangling k/d/b definitions removed.

Low-confidence list resolved: libstdc++ _S_threshold is 16 for std::sort and _S_chunk_size 7 for stable_sort; the lesson's 7 refers to stable_sort, so both are correct. JDK Arrays.sort(int[]) Javadoc says "all data sets" in 21 ("many" in 8); DualPivotQuicksort @since 1.7 * 14 has the heapsort fallback.
